Same $300 extra, different tax: side-hustle profit pays nearly double the Social Security and Medicare tax of overtime (the worker's own share).
Our math: $300 of overtime pays $22.95 in employee payroll tax (7.65%). $300 of side-hustle profit pays $42.39 in self-employment tax (15.3% on 92.35% of net earnings), because no employer pays half. This compares only the worker's own Social Security/Medicare share, before income tax: the employer also pays a matching 7.65% on overtime, and income-tax effects (half-of-SE-tax deduction, the 20% QBI deduction, the overtime deduction, your bracket) can change the bottom line. Assumes wages below the 2026 Social Security wage base ($184,500).
The federal no-tax-on-overtime deduction (2025-2028) covers only the half-time premium, up to $12,500 ($25,000 joint), phases out above $150,000 of modified AGI ($300,000 joint), and does not cut payroll tax; state rules vary.
A side hustle is taxed on profit after business expenses, and half of SE tax is deductible. A payment app or marketplace sends a 1099-K only above $20,000 and 200 transactions, but the income is taxable either way; if you expect to owe $1,000 or more, estimated taxes are due quarterly (the last 2026 payment is due Jan 15, 2027).
For scale: Bankrate's 2025 survey (fielded June 2025, released July 2025) found 27% of US adults had a side hustle, earning an average of $885 a month but a median of just $200.
Sources: US Dept. of Labor, IRS (Topics 554 and 751, Form 1040-ES, 1099-K FAQs, no-tax-on-overtime guidance), Bankrate (July 2025).
News and education, not financial advice.
